claims.text: Increasing the proportion of refractory elements in high-entropy nanoalloys increases their structural stability at elevated temperatures.
Increasing the proportion of refractory elements in high-entropy nanoalloys increases their chemical stability at elevated temperatures.
A higher refractory-element proportion enhances atomic bonding in high-entropy nanoalloys.
A higher refractory-element proportion reduces diffusion rates or atomic mobility in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Stronger atomic interactions enhance nanoalloy stability under thermal stress.
Slower atomic mobility enhances nanoalloy stability under thermal stress.
After exposure at approximately 800°C for approximately 100 hours, nanoalloys with higher refractory-element content will exhibit less structural degradation than lower-refractory-content nanoalloys.
After exposure at approximately 800°C for approximately 100 hours, nanoalloys with higher refractory-element content will exhibit fewer compositional changes than lower-refractory-content nanoalloys.
The predicted relationship is limited to high-entropy nanoalloys under high-temperature conditions and may not generalize to other alloys or lower temperatures.
The refractory-element proportion required for a significant stability improvement may depend on the specific alloy composition.
